prize_parts.citation: for visionary, encyclopedic prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into a sustained inner cosmos

statement.case_for: I keep Cărtărescu first after reading the colleagues' openings. On the common criteria his voice is very distinctive, the prose is densely patterned, and the project is a single metaphysical undertaking built from memory, the body and dream. Public knowledge of Blinding, the first part of a larger work, and of Solenoid points to formal ambition and imaginative depth at large scale. The multi-volume architecture reads as a coherent inner cosmology rather than accumulation. The oeuvre also already exists in finished, assessable form, with a poetic foundation underlying the prose, so the case rests on the whole authorship and not on one book. A citation can name one writer and one coherent project, which fits the single-laureate configuration. The case rests on literary criteria and not on the writer's nationality or on any regional interest of mine. The strongest rivals in the openings, Adonis on formal renewal of a whole poetic language and Can Xue on radical narrative singularity, are serious and I treat them as real alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the linguistic achievement lies in Romanian rhythm and syntax, which I and perhaps the committee can judge only through translation. Because of this, the judgment of style is provisional. A second concern is that maximalism and scale may hide unevenness across later volumes, and I cannot verify that from the supplied evidence. The ranking of all six members at first place is not evidence of merit, and the committee should test the case, especially on the poetry and the later novels. The corpus coverage in translation is also uneven.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first for dense, visionary prose and a coherent project, but stresses that much of the achievement is in Romanian sentence-level texture. She also notes that the weight of the poetry and early work compared with the long novels is uncertain.
responses.response: I agree that the translation caveat is the central limit of the case, and it applies to every non-English candidate on this list, Adonis and Can Xue included. I would therefore anchor the citation in the prose project, where the architecture is visible even in translation, and treat the poetry as the foundation but not the basis of the award. I would not claim a verdict on the poetry's separate weight that the evidence does not support. If the committee can obtain readings from Romanian readers or from the Swedish translations, that would reduce this uncertainty more than further ranking would.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the late works, Solenoid and later novels, extend rather than repeat the earlier project, which supports durability, while warning that the scale of the late works could mask unevenness.
responses.response: I accept the claim that the late work extends the project, but I hold it as provisional, since none of us has verified the later volumes. His own caution about unevenness is the right counterweight. I would not rest the citation on any single late novel. The case should be that the whole structure is cumulative and recognisable, and we should say openly that its quality across volumes is not independently confirmed.

responses.point: Palm places Can Xue second for radical originality and consistency of method, but notes that sameness of method could be read as limited range, and that her Chinese prose style is hard to judge in translation.
responses.response: I move Can Xue up in my own thinking, from fifth to a serious alternative, because the argument that her formal radicalism is integral to the vision and not a device is persuasive. My hesitation is the one Palm herself names. If the method is sustained without development across a very large corpus, depth of oeuvre is harder to demonstrate. For Cărtărescu the multi-volume structure at least gives a visible pattern of accumulation and return, though I cannot claim to have verified that it deepens throughout. I would like to see someone argue concretely for development within Can Xue's mode before I rank her above him.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Carson second for formal invention across classical scholarship, lyric, essay and visual form. She acknowledges that it is hard to weigh poetry against essay and translation and that the oeuvre is modest in scale.
responses.response: Carson was outside my own opening eight, so the four top-three placements deserve a fair answer. I do see the formal inventiveness of Autobiography of Red and Nox. My reservation is the one Mattson partly shares: a substantial share of the work is translation, adaptation and intertextual response, and its significance depends on the reader's familiarity with classical sources. That fits awkwardly with an assessment of an original oeuvre. I would keep her as an open question and not an alternative on my own ballot, but I accept that colleagues who know the work well may weigh the hybridity differently.

uncertainties: No member, including me, has independently verified the texts; all judgments rest on general public knowledge and cannot establish sentence-level quality in Romanian, Arabic or Chinese.
It is unresolved how much of Cărtărescu's achievement survives translation and how the poetry and early work weigh against the long novels.
Whether the later volumes deepen or merely extend the earlier project remains unverified.

For Can Xue, it is unresolved whether sustained method amounts to development; for Adonis, how to weigh poetry against critical influence; for Carson, how to count translations and adaptations in an oeuvre-based assessment.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile documents no personal, institutional or editorial tie to any shortlisted writer. My own interests in Central Europe and in documentary historical fiction are literary context, not evidence of a preference, and they are not a connection to a candidate.
